summary: I-Regexp is a deliberately limited flavor of regular expression. Its goal is interoperability, so that the same pattern behaves the same across many different regular expression libraries. It leaves out features that implementations treat differently.

plainLanguage.summary: Different pattern-matching tools speak slightly different dialects. This picks a small shared set of words that all of them understand the same way.

subtitle: A deliberately small regular expression dialect that behaves the same in many different regexp libraries.

tldr.problem: Regular expression libraries differ in their syntax and behavior, so a pattern in a data-model or query-language specification may not mean the same thing everywhere. The JSONPath working group could not find a regexp specification that was interoperable across popular libraries.
tldr.mechanism: I-Regexp defines a restricted syntax in ABNF that is a subset of XML Schema Definition (XSD) regular expressions. It supports only Boolean matching and leaves out capture groups, lookahead, backreferences, character class subtraction, multi-character escapes and Unicode blocks.
tldr.outcome: Because it is a subset of XSD regexps and maps easily onto ECMAScript, PCRE, RE2 and Ruby, implementers can support it cheaply, and its limited scope makes safe, linear-time implementations possible.

today: RFC 9485 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is intended for specifications, such as JSONPath, that need regular expressions that behave consistently across libraries.

sections.title: Introduction and Goals
sections.content:
I-Regexp is an interoperable flavor of regular expression (regexp). It offers only a Boolean matching capability: it tests whether a regexp matches a piece of text. It has no capture groups, lookahead or backreferences.

Both the I-Regexp string and the text it is matched against are sequences of Unicode scalar values, often carried as UTF-8. I-Regexp is a subset of XML Schema Definition (XSD) regular expressions.

The work was motivated by the JSONPath Working Group, which wanted regular expressions in JSONPath filters but could not find a specification that was interoperable across the popular libraries. The stated objective is to handle the vast majority of practical cases in data-model specifications and query languages. An editor surveyed regexp syntax in recently published RFCs, and all examples found should be covered, apart from multi-character escapes, for which the RFC gives workarounds.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine many friends who each play a game with slightly different rules. I-Regexp is a short rulebook of only the rules everybody already agrees on.

sections.title: The I-Regexp Syntax
sections.content:
An I-Regexp MUST conform to the ABNF grammar in the RFC. The top level is one or more branches separated by |. A branch is a series of pieces, and a piece is an atom with an optional quantifier: the star, the plus sign, the question mark or a range such as {2,4}.

An atom is an ordinary character, a character class, or a parenthesized I-Regexp. Character classes include the dot ., single-character escapes, category escapes such as \p{L} and \P{L}, and bracketed expressions such as [a-z]. The category names are the Unicode general categories: letters, marks, numbers, punctuation, separators, symbols and others, each with optional subcategories.

One extra rule applies: a character class expression is not allowed to match [^], which the grammar would otherwise parse as a positive class holding the single character ^.

The RFC describes I-Regexp as essentially an XSD regexp without character class subtraction, multi-character escapes such as \s, \S and \w, and Unicode blocks.
sections.plainLanguage: The grammar is like a Lego instruction sheet. It lists exactly which bricks you may use and how they snap together, so everybody builds the same thing.

sections.title: What Implementations Must Do
sections.content:
An I-Regexp implementation MUST be a complete implementation of the limited subset. It MUST NOT limit itself to 7- or 8-bit character sets such as ASCII, and it MUST support the Unicode character property set in character classes.

A checking implementation verifies that a supplied regexp complies with this specification and reports any problems. Checking is RECOMMENDED, because it gives users confidence that they did not accidentally use non-interoperable syntax. Low-effort implementations that map I-Regexp onto another library by simple steps may skip it, since full checking could cost more than the rest of the work. Implementations SHOULD document whether or not they are checking.

For semantics, implementations that interpret I-Regexps MUST yield the Boolean results specified in XSD.
sections.plainLanguage: A checking tool is like a spell checker. It tells you when you used a word that is not in the shared rulebook, so you can fix it before it confuses someone.

sections.title: Mapping to Other Regexp Dialects
sections.content:
This section is guidance, not a requirement. Any I-Regexp is already an XSD regexp, so for XSD the mapping is the identity function.

For ECMAScript, replace each unescaped dot outside a character class with [^\n\r], then wrap the result in ^(?: and )$. The result is interpreted as a Unicode pattern, with the u flag. For PCRE, RE2 and Ruby, do the same but enclose the result in \A(?: and )\z.

Multi-character escapes are not supported, but can usually be replaced. The RFC suggests [^ \t\n\r] for \S and [0-9] for \d. In XSD, \d means \p{Nd}, which includes digits from many writing systems and is almost certainly not what IETF publications want. The legacy reference \p{IsBasicLatin} can become [\u0000-\u007f].
sections.plainLanguage: If your tool speaks a slightly different dialect, there are simple translation tips. Mostly you add a couple of marks at the start and end so the whole text has to match.

sections.title: Why It Is Limited
sections.content:
Regular expressions were meant to describe a formal language for a Boolean matching function. Over time they gained parsing functions to extract and replace parts of matched text. The RFC says this accretion of features made parsing-regexp libraries more susceptible to bugs and surprising performance degradation, which can be exploited in denial-of-service attacks by someone who controls the submitted regexp.

I-Regexp trades features for interoperability and lower exposure to such attacks. XSD regexps are fairly easy to implement or map, with three notable exceptions that I-Regexp omits or flags: character class subtraction, which is mostly absent from parsing dialects; multi-character escapes such as \d, \w and \s, which vary widely between flavors; and Unicode tables for constructs like \p{Nd}. Libraries in severely constrained environments may not be able to support conformance because they lack those tables.
sections.plainLanguage: A Swiss army knife with fifty tools can jam or hurt you. A knife with only a blade is simpler, and everyone knows how it works.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Implementations should keep in mind the security considerations of the UTF-8 specification, RFC 3629. Complex regexp libraries may contain exploitable bugs that can cause crashes and remote code execution, and their performance can be hard to predict, so an attacker-controlled expensive regexp can overload a system.

I-Regexps are designed so that implementations can be resilient to both threats. Implementations focused on the subset can, with care, run in linear time and space in the input and detect when they would not. Non-checking implementations inherit the weaknesses of whatever engine they use, so a checking implementation is still RECOMMENDED.

Range quantifiers such as a{2,4} are a particular challenge. Implementations may disallow nesting, as in (a{2,4}){2,4}, may disallow very large ranges such as a{20,200000}, or may detect and reject excessive resource use. Implementations that evaluate regexps from untrusted sources need to be robust here, and are encouraged to check whether library mitigations are configurable and to document their own robustness.
sections.plainLanguage: If a stranger can hand you a puzzle, they might hand you one that takes forever. Keeping the puzzle language small makes it easier to say no to the nasty ones.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: This document has no IANA actions. I-Regexp is a syntax and set of semantics that other specifications can reference, so there is nothing to register.
sections.plainLanguage: There is no list to add to, so nobody has to update any official registry.

items.title: Character class subtraction
items.text: Mostly absent from parsing-regexp dialects, so omitted.

items.title: Multi-character escapes
items.text: \s, \S, \w and similar vary between flavors, so omitted.

items.title: Unicode blocks
items.text: Not part of the subset; \p{IsBasicLatin} becomes [\u0000-\u007f].
